messages.subject: Solving ODEs for time arrays of different sizes
parts:
Dear Stan team and users,

I'm trying to analyse population pharmacokinetic data (drug concentration-time data for several individuals) using a mixed-effects model defined with two ODEs. Since the subjects in the dataset have time vectors of different lengths, I'm struggling to provide individual time vectors (all appended in one "TIME" vector) adequately for the "integrate_ode" function.
I usually deal with this issue using a list of vectors in R or cells in MATLAB but I believe Stan doesn't support such data structures? I thus tried:
  • to solve the equations for each time point for each subject, i.e. for each element of the "TIME" vector (see "transformed parameters" block in PK_ODE.stan), but the time argument in the "integrate_ode" function has to be an array of real numbers and can apparently not be a single real number: 


  • to provide the time vector for each individual using the "segment" function (see  "transformed parameters" block in PK_ODE_02.stan), but the time argument in the "integrate_ode" function has to be pure data:



Any suggestion to deal with this problem?

Many thanks in advance for your help.

BW,
Thierry Wendling

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Solving ODEs for time arrays of different sizes
parts:
Stan has arrays of vectors, but they all have to be the same size.
Adding ragged arrays is a fairly big project and one of the things on
our current round of grant proposals :-) Along with sparse matrices.
And structured matrices.

For now, you need to use an indexing hack. There are various examples
in the manual, but they need to be updated to use our slicing functions.
I should really add a whole chapter, so I added it to the next-manual to-do list:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1081#issuecomment-62575137

The short answer is to do something like this:

int[N] size;
real[K] values;

int pos;
pos <- 1;
for (n in 1:N) {
real[sizes[n]] value_n;
values_n <- slice(values, pos, size[n]);

... do what you want with values_n ...

For instance, if you had the equivalent of R's list(c(10,9),c(8,7,6),c(5))
you would have

size = { 2, 3, 1 }
values = { 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5 }

- Bob

P.S. Given that we just rolled out the ODE solver, we'd be
interested in getting feedback on how it works. We're still encountering
some issues with long integration times when the sampler gets into
regions of the posterior that stiffen the ODE. One of our highest-priority
issues at the moment is dealing with this issue --- our plan is to plug in
lsoda as the general integrator (workhorse of deSolve in R), but any advice
on integrators, etc., is appreciated --- none of us are specialists in
general numerical integration.

parts:
Hi Thierry,

I too have been struggling with the ODE solver in Stan 2.5. I found I need to carefully constrain the parameters to prevent combinations of value that result in stiff equations or near discontinuities. When I allowed parameters to be unconstrained or have large supports, Stan would often attempt some extreme parameter values. The result is that the solver would spin for hours without a result. 

Bob et al: consider this a plea to implement a version of integrate_ode that provides arguments for setting error tolerances and limits on step size or number of steps--and that will exit with an error message when such limits are exceeded rather than apparently going into an infinite loop.

I have also dealt with the problem of analyzing popPK data from patients with different numbers of observations. The attached Stan code illustrates the approach I used. It implements a linear 2 compartment model with 1st order absorption--a testing exercise since it is solvable analytically. The data set is based on NONMEM conventions for representing dose events. The corresponding R code and data set is attached. This is simulated data I have used at Metrum for teaching an introductory Bayesian analysis course using WinBUGS.

Cheers,
Bill

Bill --- your plea's already been anticipated. I
ran into the same problem a few days ago and filed a
feature request:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1127

Bill's diagnosis is correct --- you need to ensure the parameters
don't wander into stiff territory.

We are definitely going to

A. include a variable stiffness solver like lsoda; already
on our near term to-do list, and

B. allow user control of absolute and relative tolerances.

See the discussion of the issue for reasons we don't just want
to throttle number of steps (short answer --- same reason we
don't want to limit number of leapfrog steps in the HMC integrator ---
we don't want to bias results).

For now, I found the following two steps should help:

1. lowering initial step size to something like .01 or even
lower

2. increasing accept target to 0.9 or even higher

In RStan, this will look like:

fit <- stan("soil_incubation.stan",
data=c("totalC_t0", "t0", "T", "ts", "eCO2"),
control=list(adapt_delta=0.95,
stepsize=0.01),
chains=4, iter=4000, seed=1234);

Without the control parameters, the integrator would just
grind to a halt.

(1) will force Stan to take small steps to start and (2) will
make sure the step size doesn't grow too much during adaptation (small
step sizes are needed to guarantee high acceptance rates).
Small step sizes allow Stan's HMC simulation to follow the curvature
of the posterior more closely and avoid low density areas that tend
to be stiff.

parts:
As things stand in Stan 2.5, our ODE solver is very inefficient
if there is stiffness in the diff eqs. If you're finding a huge
difference in iteration times, what you may be seeing is the
parameters taking on values that induce stiffness in the ODE.

It also looks like your ODE is introducing a discontinuity. The
solver may have trouble integrating past this point:

tinf <- dosing[1];
if (t <= tinf)
rate <- dosing[2];
else
rate <- 0;

dydt[1] <- rate - (k10+k12)*y[1] + k21*y[2];
dydt[2] <- k12 *y[1] - k21*y[2];

What we've done before is run the integrator between dosing
events rather than trying to run it across dosing events.

Even with what you have it's more efficient to rewrite as:

tinf <- dosing[1];
if (t <= tinf) {
rate <- dosing[2];
dydt[1] <- rate - (k10 + k12) * y[1] + k21 * y[2];
} else {
dydt[1] <- -(k10 + k12) * y[1] + k21 * y[2];
}

You also have some pretty diffuse priors:


// Model for the priors
logmu ~ normal(3,100);
gamma ~ normal(1,10);
tau_OMEGA ~ cauchy(0,2);
sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);

If you can tighten these up with knowledge about the expected
answers, it can make a big difference to Stan (even in models w/o
diff eqs).

This:
for (i in 1:Nsub)

e_logtheta[i] ~ normal(0,1);

would be more efficient in vector form as:

e_logtheta ~ normal(0,1);

Also, the algebra you have in transformed parameters may be
leading to numerical difficulies in that you're taking exp() and
then log(), which is a bad-news roundtrip (not in theory, but with
floating point arithmetic as implemented on computers). For
example, this:

theta[i,1] <- exp( logmu[1] + tau_OMEGA[1] * e_logtheta[i,1] );

coupled with:

LNIPRED[j] <- log(sol[1,1]/theta[ID[j],2]);

is bad news numerically compared to this:

log_theta[i,1] <- logmu[1] + tau_OMEGA[1] * e_logtheta[i,1];

...

LNIPRED[j] <- log(sol[1,1]) - theta_log[ID[j],2]);

and so on for the other values. The general rule is don't ever apply
exp if you can help it, and if you apply log, never apply it to values near
1 (use log1p or log1m instead).

- Bob
